summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach the island only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills rather than through inherited Westminster statute, so the island's record must be read on its own terms.

Partner recognition is established. Same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act, reported on 28 July 2016, and the first conversion of a civil partnership into a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships, legal since 2011, convert without a second ceremony, which indicates a routine registration process rather than discretionary approval.

The primary legislative record of that reform sits in Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016, which records the Legislative Council's Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016. The reform also had stated political sponsorship: on 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.

Non-discrimination protection on the island was first legislated in the employment sphere. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island with United Kingdom human-rights law.

Nothing in this inventory documents a gender-recognition procedure, identity-document marker rules, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans visitor's status, hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, or facility access rules. Those questions are not evidenced here rather than shown to be absent from Manx law, and a visitor should treat them as open.
tangentialFactors:
The island's equality architecture has been built in stages, and the sequence matters for expectation-setting. Employment protection on sexual-orientation grounds came a decade before the marriage debate, in 2005; the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act and the Equality Bill 2016 followed in a single legislative session. Both were framed by Tynwald rather than imposed from Westminster.

The proximity of the Equality Bill 2016 to the marriage legislation indicates that discrimination protection and relationship recognition were handled as one reform programme, though the inventory does not record the substantive content of the Equality Bill.

Detention capacity on the island is limited to a single institution. Isle of Man Prison at Jurby, a GBP 41.7m facility on the former RAF Jurby site, has been fully operational since 14 August 2008 and is run by the Isle of Man Prison Service, with separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders, vulnerable prisoners and a segregation unit.
localsOnly:
Employees on the island have had a statutory ground of challenge against dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds since the House of Keys adopted the Employment Bill amendment on 30 November 2005, an amendment tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran.

Resident couples have had civil partnerships since 2011 and same-sex marriage since the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act received Royal Assent, reported on 28 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships convert to marriage without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force.

The Equality Bill 2016 was before the Legislative Council on 26 April 2016, the same sitting that carried the Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: this inventory contains no evidence on a gender-recognition procedure, on marker or sex-entry rules for passports, licences or birth certificates, or on any requirement that could disclose a trans person's status at the border. Whether such provisions exist in Manx law is not sourced here.

Unresolved: no hate-crime provision covering gender identity is documented, and no rule governing access to sex-separated facilities, shelters or services is documented. The 2005 employment amendment as reported addresses sexual-orientation grounds only; whether gender identity is a protected characteristic under the island's subsequent equality legislation is not sourced in this inventory.

Unresolved: the Isle of Man Prison inventory records no birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific segregation practice, so the prison-housing axis yields no usable finding either way.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 does not extend to the Isle of Man automatically; extension would require an Order in Council, and no such extension of the 2025 single-sex-services code is recorded here.
